prompt: Which of these does a headless Chromium skip?

choices.text: Running the page's scripts
choices.why: It runs them: lesson 1's smoke test counted eight cards that only a script draws.

choices.text: Showing the painted page on a screen, which it does not have
choices.why: Right. It parses, runs, lays out and paints; the pixels go to memory, where a screenshot can read them.

choices.text: Computing the layout of the page
choices.why: Lesson 7 measured an overflow of forty pixels headless, which needs a layout.

choices.text: Fetching the files the page links to, like its scripts
choices.why: Every request a page makes is made headless too; the Network panel of lesson 1 would show the same list.

prompt: `modes.mjs shell` prints `ownWindow: '800x600'` and `viewport: '1280x720'`. Why two sizes?

choices.text: The first is the screen, the second the window
choices.why: There is no screen at all; both are sizes the browser and Playwright chose.

choices.text: Window invented; viewport set by Playwright
choices.why: Right. A page made with `viewport: null` measures the invented window; a test's page gets 1280 by 720.

choices.text: The page was zoomed out
choices.why: Nothing changed the zoom; the two sizes come from two different settings.

choices.text: The shell rounds sizes down
choices.why: No rounding is involved: 800 by 600 is the shell's own default window.

prompt: Inside a page driven by a program, the property `navigator.___` was `true` in all three modes.
hint: It is the flag a site's script reads to tell automation apart.

prompt: With `headless: true` and no `channel`, which program does Playwright 1.56 start?

choices.text: The full Chromium, with its window switched off
choices.why: That is what `channel: 'chromium'` asks for; the default is the other one.

choices.text: The Google Chrome installed on the computer
choices.why: That is `channel: 'chrome'`, from lesson 10; the default uses Playwright's own download.

choices.text: `headless_shell`
choices.why: Right. The launch line names `chromium_headless_shell-1194/chrome-linux/headless_shell`.

choices.text: Whichever build of Chromium was downloaded most recently
choices.why: Playwright asks for one exact build per version, 1194 for 1.56, and the choice of program follows the options.

prompt: A guide tells you to pass `--headless=old` to Chrome 141 through Selenium. Chromedriver answers that the user data directory is probably in use. What is the cause?

choices.text: Another Chrome is running with the same profile
choices.why: That is what the message guesses; started by hand, Chrome says the old mode was removed.

choices.text: The old mode is gone from Chrome, which exits
choices.why: Right. Chrome's own message points to new headless or to chrome-headless-shell, and chromedriver only saw a browser that never answered.

choices.text: Selenium needs the argument spelled `-headless`
choices.why: The single hyphen is Firefox's spelling; Chrome accepts `--headless` and `--headless=new`.

choices.text: Chromedriver 141 cannot run headless at all
choices.why: The same driver ran `--headless=new` a line earlier and opened the deals page.

prompt: Which of these differed between the headless shell and new headless on this machine? Choose every one.

choices.text: The version digits in the user agent
choices.why: Yes: `141.0.7390.37` from the shell, `141.0.0.0` from the full browser.

choices.text: The size of the window the browser invented
choices.why: Yes: 800 by 600 against 780 by 493.

choices.text: The word `HeadlessChrome` in the user agent
choices.why: Both sent it; only a window removes it.

choices.text: The viewport a test's page gets
choices.why: 1280 by 720 in both: Playwright sets it whatever the window is.

prompt: How does a Selenium test ask Firefox to run without a window?

choices.text: `new firefox.Options().addArguments('-headless')`
choices.why: Right. It is Firefox's own argument, with one hyphen, and it travels in `moz:firefoxOptions`.

choices.text: `--headless=new`
choices.why: That is Chrome's spelling; Selenium hands arguments over untranslated.

choices.text: `new firefox.Options().headless()`
choices.why: The changelog removes that method in 4.17.0; on 4.51.0 the call is an error.

choices.text: Nothing: geckodriver starts Firefox headless by default
choices.why: Selenium opens a window unless told otherwise, in Firefox as in Chrome.

prompt: A colleague asks what Firefox's user agent says in headless mode, and whether the deals page would send it the phone page. What can this lesson tell them?

choices.text: That it contains `HeadlessFirefox`, as Chromium's says `HeadlessChrome`
choices.why: No Firefox ran for this lesson, so no string was seen; that would be an invented answer.

choices.text: Nothing about the string; but a desktop Firefox sends no `Mobile`, so the desktop page
choices.why: Right. The string has to be read from a run; the page's rule only looks for one word, and the lesson says which.

choices.text: That it is identical to Chrome's
choices.why: Different browsers name themselves differently, and nothing here measured Firefox.

choices.text: That the phone page, because headless browsers are treated as small screens
choices.why: The server reads only the user agent, and Chromium's headless string got the desktop page.

prompt: What does `xvfb-run` give a browser on a server with no screen?

choices.text: A remote screen that a person can watch
choices.why: Xvfb draws into memory; nobody sees it unless something takes a picture of it.

choices.text: A faster headless mode
choices.why: The browser runs headed under it; the user agent loses `HeadlessChrome`.

choices.text: A display in memory
choices.why: Right. It sets `DISPLAY`, runs the command and stops the server afterwards.

choices.text: A copy of Chromium built without the window code
choices.why: That describes the headless shell; Xvfb is not a browser.

prompt: Under `xvfb-run` with its default screen, how many pixels wide was the window Chromium opened for itself?
hint: The screen was 1280 by 1024; the window was smaller.

prompt: A Selenium suite passes headed on a laptop and fails headless on the build server: an element below the fold is never in view. What does the lesson point at first?

choices.text: Selenium sets no viewport; the window is the page
choices.why: Right. Headless Chrome gave Selenium 780 by 441 here, and under Xvfb 1050 by 865; set the window size in the suite.

choices.text: The build server's Chrome is a different build from the laptop's
choices.why: Possible in general, but a version difference would not move one element out of view on its own.

choices.text: Headless Chrome does not compute the layout below the fold
choices.why: It does; that is why a size can cut a card in the first place.

choices.text: The test needs a longer wait
choices.why: The element is there; it is outside a smaller window, and waiting will not make the window taller.

prompt: The test with `test.use({ viewport: null })` passed in the shell and headed, and failed in new headless. Why?

choices.text: New headless renders the grid with a different engine
choices.why: Both are Chromium 141; the grid followed the window it was given.

choices.text: Its invented window is 493 tall, and the card ends below that
choices.why: Right. With no viewport the page is the window, and only that window cuts Pineapple.

choices.text: The shop answered new headless more slowly, so the grid was not drawn yet
choices.why: The count of eight passed first, so the products were there; the failure is about where they were.

choices.text: `toBeInViewport` cannot measure anything in a browser without a screen
choices.why: It passed in the shell, which has no screen either.

prompt: A team's own site shows a challenge page to anything whose `navigator.webdriver` is `true`. Their suite is red in the test environment. By the lesson, what should they do?

choices.text: Set a person's user agent in the suite so that the check is never triggered
choices.why: A `userAgent` does not change `navigator.webdriver`, and a suite pretending to be a person is a sign the environment is wrong.

choices.text: Run the suite headed under Xvfb
choices.why: The flag was `true` headed too; the window does not change it.

choices.text: Ask for a test-environment switch, and test that it is off in production
choices.why: Right. The rule stays visible, and a test keeps the exception from leaking out.

choices.text: Delete the tests that hit the challenge page and keep the rest green
choices.why: That stops testing the site at all; the challenge is a rule to make explicit, not a reason to look away.

prompt: Screenshots taken headed on a laptop are compared, on the build server, with screenshots taken headless. They fail on pixels nobody can see a problem in. What does the lesson name as the cause to check first?

choices.text: Headless paints only the part of the page that is visible in the window
choices.why: It paints what a headed browser paints; the pixels went to memory.

choices.text: The fonts: `system-ui` is a different family on each machine
choices.why: Right. Text of a different width wraps elsewhere; take the reference on the same kind of machine and mode.

choices.text: Screenshots taken in headless mode differ randomly from one run to the next
choices.why: Nothing random is involved; two machines draw two pages.

choices.text: The build server has a different shop
choices.why: Both ran the same project; the difference is the machine around the browser.

prompt: Each run of the five files took between 12 and 18 seconds. Why could no mode remove most of that time?

choices.text: The browser starts again before every test
choices.why: One worker starts its browser once and reuses it; each test gets a new page, not a new browser.

choices.text: Most of the time is the shop's own waits
choices.why: Right. The slow search, the late script and an expected failure's six seconds are the shop and the test, in every mode.

choices.text: Playwright ran the tests in parallel
choices.why: Every run used `--workers 1`, one test after another.

choices.text: Laying out each page is the slow part, and every mode does it
choices.why: Layout is part of each test's few hundred milliseconds; the seconds are in the waits.

prompt: A suite of a thousand short tests, each opening a page and clicking once, moves from headed to headless. Compared with this lesson's suite, what do you expect?

choices.text: No change at all, because this lesson measured almost no difference
choices.why: This suite is dominated by waits; a suite of short tests spends a larger share in the browser.

choices.text: A larger share saved, and a number to measure rather than assume
choices.why: Right. The saving comes from the browser's share of the time, which is larger here; the size of it still needs a run.

choices.text: Ten times faster, the usual figure
choices.why: The lesson's point is that such figures are repeated, not measured.

choices.text: Slower, since a headless browser has to repeat the layout for every page
choices.why: Headless lays out once per page, like headed; it only skips the screen.

prompt: Match each way of starting Chromium to what its user agent said on this machine.
A test passes on your laptop and fails on the build server. Put the investigation in the lesson's order.
items: Find out which program and mode the server launches
Print the sizes and user agent that mode gives the page
Reproduce the failure in that mode on your own machine
Pin what the test depended on, such as the viewport
trap: Pinning first guesses at the cause; the launch line and the probe say what to pin.

prompt: A build server will only ever run `npx playwright test` with the project's default configuration. Which install fits it, by the lesson?

choices.text: `npx playwright install --no-shell chromium`
choices.why: That keeps the full browser and drops the shell, which is exactly what the default needs.

choices.text: `npx playwright install --only-shell chromium`
choices.why: Right. Headless with no channel launches the shell, so the 597 MB browser would sit unused.

choices.text: `sudo apt-get install xvfb`, and nothing else
choices.why: Xvfb gives a display to a headed run; this server runs headless and still needs a browser.

choices.text: `npx playwright install --with-deps chromium firefox`
choices.why: It downloads Firefox and the full Chromium too, plus system packages; the default configuration uses only the shell.
